new_statements.rule_in_words: Final syllable never stressed (except in pause and in enclitic combinations). Stress the penult if it is heavy (long vowel or closed); if the penult is light, the antepenult; if the antepenult is also light in a word of four or more syllables, stress retracts as far leftward as possible, i.e. to the initial syllable (ká-ta-ba-tā, más-'a-la-tun). This is the unbounded-retraction ('Wright') position.
new_statements.exceptions: § 28 (a): pausal forms of §§ 29-30 keep their accent (ya-ḳūl, kā-nūn, mu'-mi-nīn), but words ending in -iyun, -uwun, -ā'un etc. throw the accent back as far as possible in pause (Ḳo-ra-šī-yun > Ḳó-ra-šī); (b) monosyllables combined with the proclitics 'a-, bi-, ka-, li-, wa-, fa- keep their accent ('a-lā́, bi-mā́, wa-lám); the only old-Arabic exception is the interrogative enclitic mā (bí-ma, lí-ma). § 31 Rem.: deviations 'in Egypt and among the Bèdawīn' referred to compilation, Wallin and Spitta.

new_statements.quote: § 9. The tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: Counting back from the end of the word ('forward' in Arabic script direction), stress the first long syllable met, i.e. the rightmost heavy syllable (closed or long-vowelled: istánkara, mámlakatun, fárdun), a final simple long syllable (CVV or CVC) not counting as heavy (tamámtumā); if the word has no such syllable, stress the initial syllable (ḍáraba). No window is stated, so the default is unbounded retraction to the initial syllable, as in Wright. § 8 (p. 16) defines short (CV), long (CVV, CVC) and 'doubly long' (CVVC) syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: A syllable with connective (prosthetic) alif cannot bear the accent (iftáʻala, not *ʼíftaʻala); the proclitic particles wa-, fa- do not alter the accent (famášā). Final superheavy syllables are not discussed explicitly (only 'simple' long finals are excluded).

It stresses the last strong cluster of the word, with one exception to be noted in Chapter XII. If there is no strong cluster, stress is placed according to the Romance Stress Rule for all categories of speech. This may be illustrated by the following examples. 13) dáxxal+at kitā́b+u+n kátab+at / daxál+tu kā́tib+u+n malík+at+u+n / sāfár+tu katab+ú+hu málik+u+n / qábl+a sā́far+a fáqaṭ / daxxál+tu+hu kātib+í+na lán. readall_conflicts: The three readable works agree that Standard/Classical Arabic stress is weight-sensitive (heavy penult stressed, else antepenult, final syllable normally unstressed) but split on the leftmost limit, exactly the split the existing Watson 2011 statement reports. Wright (1859/1896, §31, p. 28) and Socin (1885, § 9, p. 16) let stress retract without bound to the first syllable when no non-final heavy syllable is available within reach (Wright: 'In other cases the accent is thrown as far back as possible; as ká-ta-ba-tā, más-'a-la-tun'; Socin: 'when there is no long syllable, the accent is on the first syllable'), whereas Brame (1970, p. 367, rule 14) bounds stress to the last three syllables, so 'a strong cluster followed by three weak syllables' is skipped and the antepenult is stressed (yādár+a+hu, malík+at+u+n). On the same word the two give different outputs: Wright ká-ta-ba-tā versus Brame kàtabatā́ (p. 445, dual -ā stressed with secondary stress on the initial). Wright's four-syllable examples with a heavy initial (más-'a-la-tun) would receive antepenultimate stress (mas'álatun) under Brame's rule. Neither Wright nor Socin mentions secondary stress; Brame does. Yoshida 1993 and Kremers 2003 could not be opened.

sources.quote: The rule of stress assignment of Arabic is very much like the Romance Stress Rule. It stresses the last strong cluster of the word, with one exception to be noted in Chapter XII. If there is no strong cluster, stress is placed according to the Romance Stress Rule for all categories of speech. This may be illustrated by the following examples. 13) dáxxal+at kitā́b+u+n kátab+at / daxál+tu kā́tib+u+n malík+at+u+n / sāfár+tu katab+ú+hu málik+u+n / qábl+a sā́far+a fáqaṭ / daxxál+tu+hu kātib+í+na lán. Thus, the rule of Stress Assignment is essentially 14). 14) Stress Assignment: V --> [1 stress] / __C₀((VC)VC₀¹)Ψ. This rule predicts that should a form contain a strong cluster followed by three weak syllables, stress will be assigned on the weak syllable following the strong cluster, not on the strong cluster syllable. This prediction is borne out by examples such as yādár+a+hu, 'he left it', ya+ftátiḥ+u, 'he opens it (ceremoniously)'
